title: How MadCap Flare's Limitations Compound as Documentation Scales (+ How to Fix It)
summary: Long builds, snippet bloat, and slow localization: see how MadCap Flare’s problems compound as documentation scales, and when switching makes sense.
body_markdown:
Project bloat, inconsistent content reuse, and slow localization usually creep up gradually. Learn why these problems compound as your documentation scales in MadCap Flare and when it may be time to move on.


---


MadCap Flare makes a lot of sense when your documentation team is small. Single-sourcing helps you keep outputs consistent, and a grandfathered license (where you pay under $10,000 for a few author seats) means the cost is easier to justify.


But every tool reaches a point where workarounds simply stop working and the features that once saved time can create more work to maintain. More writers bring different authoring habits, more content makes reuse harder to manage, and more languages add to publishing time.


Eventually, the effort required to keep everything working can outweigh the time the tool saves.


*As documentation grows, coordination and publishing overhead can eat into productivity gains*


An ex-Madcap Flare customer described their experience with MadCap Flare as shifting from appreciation to frustration, saying the tool became a burden for their team. Here’s how they put it:


**“I definitely had a love-hate relationship with Flare at one point, but I think the love is gone at this point. Flare is really a burden for us right now.”**


While these challenges appear gradually, they typically escalate across distinct organizational milestones. As headcount and document volume expand, what begins as manageable friction quickly spirals into an architectural bottleneck. Here is how those challenges compound across three operational thresholds.


## Threshold 1 (1–3 Writers, <500 documents) #


**When a small team can work around MadCap Flare’s quirks**


MadCap Flare has plenty to offer a small documentation team. A few writers can reuse content across web and PDF outputs, share styles, and manage a project without much coordination. The team can also work around Flare's limitations through informal conversations and shared knowledge.


There are trade-offs, though. New writers need time to both learn XML-based authoring and understand the project structure and how those conditions work before they can make changes confidently. In larger projects, undocumented rules and custom publishing steps can make that learning curve even steeper.


Publishing an update means rebuilding the output and waiting for it to finish. Plus, if you're running purely on the desktop app without cloud governance layers, there are essentially no guardrails. Any writer can tweak a global stylesheet, variable, or conditional tag—and accidentally break output across the whole project.


[Source](https://www.reddit.com/r/technicalwriting/comments/1bw7nax/comment/lu92hsr/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=web3x&utm_name=web3xcss&utm_term=1&utm_content=share_button)


These issues take time to manage, but a small team can usually keep them under control. The benefits of single-sourcing, flexible authoring, and an affordable legacy license may still outweigh the extra effort. You know the workarounds, and they get the job done.


As the team grows, though, those workarounds become harder to sustain. More writers bring different habits, more documents create more opportunities for inconsistencies, and the effort required to keep the project organized starts to add up.


## Threshold 2 (4+ Writers, 500+ documents) #


**When flexibility comes at the cost of consistency**


As more writers join the team, informal coordination becomes harder to manage. Each writer develops their own approach to snippets and conditional tags. One might turn a single sentence into a snippet, while another reserves snippets for entire pages. These differences leave the project with overlapping content and increasingly complex conditions.


*When every writer has their own rules for snippets.*


During a conversation, one ex-MadCap-Flare user described how such inconsistent practices contributed to project bloat:


**“We've got maybe 80% overlap of content in a snippet, for instance, but then there's that 20% that is only for web and 20% that's only for mobile... Because the team all has different approaches with those tools, it’s a big part of what’s bloated the project. We have one writer who, if he reuses a sentence, wants it to be a snippet. Other writers need to see it across multiple topics or huge blocks of content to warrant or justify making it into snippets.”**


Similarly, other problems that seemed manageable with a small team start to add up here:


- **Longer build times:** Generating a full output can take longer, particularly when shared snippets, conditional content, and cross-references need to be processed. With 500+ articles and multiple targets to maintain, full builds can slow down validation and publishing.
- **More complex reviews:** Reviewers need to check how changes affect shared snippets, conditional tags, and multiple topics. Without a straightforward review workflow, catching inconsistencies and coordinating edits takes more time.


## Threshold 3 (Multiple products, platforms, and languages) #


**When overhead compounds exponentially with every new update**


The problems from Threshold 2 get harder to manage as the documentation expands across products, platforms, and languages. This is where you start seeing **exponential overhead** .


As documentation expands across products and platforms, build times can become a bottleneck. In MadCap Flare, each additional language adds more targets to build and maintain. As the number of targets grows, these repeated build cycles can slow down the entire publishing process.


**Consider a project with 18 targets covering different platforms and product tiers. Translating those outputs into five languages brings the total to 90 targets.**


The impact can become more pronounced when documentation expands across outputs and languages. In one case, a help project supported three outputs and two translated languages. Publishing took so long that the team decided to hold off on further localization.


***“\[O\]ne of our help projects is translated into two languages and that… exponentially increases the build time… so I have strictly told our product team ‘no’ \[to further localization\] until we’re no longer using Flare \[and\] Lingo.”***


Build times make the problem worse. Flare requires writers to build an output before publishing and checking their changes. As projects grow, each build has more content, conditions, and cross-references to process. Repeat this across dozens of targets, and routine updates take longer to release.


At this stage, teams spend more time maintaining the documentation project and publishing updates. Adding languages becomes harder to justify, builds take longer, and keeping context-sensitive help aligned requires ongoing coordination between writers and developers.


Eventually, your team has to decide whether the time spent managing MadCap Flare is still worth it.


## Breaking the MadCap Flare ceiling: Why enterprise teams migrate to Archbee #


If your team has outgrown MadCap Flare's workflows, switching to Archbee can help remove the bottlenecks that come with scaling documentation. You can publish updates without local builds, bring writers and developers into a shared workflow through 2-way Git sync, and manage translations alongside your source content.


That means less time maintaining the documentation project and more time keeping your docs accurate and up to date.


### Create, review and publish docs without build bottlenecks #


With a small team, waiting for a local MadCap Flare build is a minor inconvenience. But as the project grows, builds take longer, reviews involve more people, and every update takes more coordination.


Archbee brings document creation, reviews, and publishing into the same platform. Writers can edit documentation in a browser, share drafts for review, and publish approved changes without running a local build.


Archbee also supports reusable blocks, but unlike MadCap Flare, you can’t turn existing text into a snippet on the go. Instead, you create reusable blocks in a dedicated section. This extra step encourages writers to think about what’s worth reusing, rather than turning every other sentence into a snippet by default.


Overall, this gives your team a more direct and structured path from creating to publishing. They can review and release updates without spending as much time managing builds.

### Get new writers contributing sooner #


Archbee uses a block-based editor that supports both Markdown and visual editing. Writers can add headings, tables, code blocks, API endpoints, and diagrams without working directly with XML. You can also paste Markdown into the editor and continue editing the content visually.


For teams managing documentation for different products or audiences, Archbee supports reusable blocks and conditional content. Writers can maintain shared content in one place and control which content appears for different audiences.


More importantly, transitioning away from MadCap Flare doesn't mean abandoning content reuse. You’re simply cleaning up the technical debt. Instead of brittle, sentence-level snippets that lead to semantic drift and broken syntax, teams shift to modular, component-level blocks. This gives you audience-specific conditioning and multi-page updates without the compounding overhead of untangling micro-dependencies.

### Keep writers and developers on the same page with two-way Git sync #


When technical writers and developers work in different environments, keeping documentation aligned with the code can take extra coordination. Writers may edit topics in Flare while developers update documentation files in GitHub. Both sides need to track changes and resolve conflicts when they touch the same content.


Archbee's two-way Git sync lets teams work in either environment. Writers can edit in Archbee, while developers continue working in the Git tool. Changes from Archbee can go through a pull request, where the team reviews and merges them. So, your Git repo remains the source of truth, and merged changes sync back to Archbee.


*Let writers and developers work in their preferred format, whether Markdown or a visual editor*


This gives writers and developers a shared workflow without requiring everyone to use the same editor. Pull requests and reviews still matter, but teams can coordinate documentation changes alongside their code changes.


### Manage translations alongside source content #


Publishing time, as we saw earlier, can become a reason to hold back on adding languages. Archbee lets writers manage translated documentation alongside the source content. They can create language versions of a space, keep them organized, and use AI to translate documents in a space automatically.


Also, when you update your documentation for new feature releases or product updates, you can trigger auto-translations for all languages in your help documentation. Translations are created in draft mode, so your team can review and approve changes before they go live. This gives your team control and helps prevent AI-generated errors from reaching readers.


*Manage translated documentation alongside the source content with Archbee*


## When does switching become worth the cost? #

It also helps to look at what's slowing your team down today. Are long build times delaying updates or are publishing bottlenecks holding back localization? These are all signs that your current setup may no longer meet your needs. Looking at these challenges alongside what a new platform offers can help you decide whether switching makes sense for your team.

## Frequently Asked Questions


MadCap Flare lets writers control snippets, conditional tags, variables, and output settings. With more writers, those features can be used inconsistently. The team then spends more time reviewing shared content, resolving conflicting edits, and maintaining the project as the number of topics and outputs grows.


Project bloat in MadCap Flare often starts when writers follow different rules for content reuse. One writer might turn a sentence into a snippet, while another creates snippets only for entire sections. This can leave overlapping content, nested conditions, and more dependencies to check whenever someone updates a topic.


Yes, but the workflow depends on your setup. Flare Online offers browser-based reviews, but writers have to use Flare Desktop for advanced authoring and Flare Online for reviews.


MadCap Flare integrates with Git to track file changes, manage versions, and merge edits. Git doesn't provide a separate collaborative authoring environment, though. Writers still author primarily in Flare Desktop, then commit and sync their changes.


MadCap Flare doesn't offer incremental compilation, so it can require a full build of a target after a small content change. Each additional language and output creates more targets to build and publish. For teams managing dozens of targets, those repeated build cycles can delay routine documentation updates.


Start by identifying the content and features your team relies on, including snippets, variables, conditional text, links, and output formats. These may not transfer directly to a new platform. Test a representative sample first, check what needs rebuilding, and validate the migrated content before switching your live documentation.


Archbee is worth considering if your team wants browser-based authoring, publishing without Flare's traditional local build workflow, GitHub sync, and built-in tools for managing language versions. This enables writers and engineers to ship documentation faster with a dramatically simpler learning curve.
